TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

       Whitis Land Investments, LP (“Whitis”) timely files this Initial Post-Hearing Brief
under SOAH Order No. 6.
                            SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT

       Because of the scale of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan and the aggressive statutory
deadline, nothing in this case should be treated as business as usual. To the Joint Applicants,
the conflux of these elements produced an application that presumed success without
independently establishing mandatory criteria for the project’s need. To the Intervenors, none
of whom receive an identifiable benefit from the construction of this 765kV line, the PURA
routing factors have been thrown out of balance through the legislature’s decision to sacrifice
some community protections for the benefit of the oil and gas industry in the Permian Basin.

        Even if the ALJs find that the project is needed, the route recommendation should not
default to traditional factor weighting. On this record, the proper balance is a route that gives
real weight to community values, existing and future land use, and preserving as much of the
original character of the affected land as possible. No other set of priorities comes close to
compensating for the burden placed on affected landowners.

 I.        INTRODUCTION
        Whitis owns a 1,272-acre ranch in Bell County, Texas, crossed by Links E13, E52, and
F1. The property contains approximately 1.5 miles of Buttermilk Creek and Salado Creek. 2
      1

The property also contains countless archeological artifacts due to the presence of the creeks.3
Near the intersection of Links E13, E52, and F1 lies a 2,800-foot grass airstrip, which has been
registered with the Federal Aviation Administration prior to the application date.4 The airstrip
has been incorporated into a multi-phase residential subdivision, designed to yield
approximately 3,800 single family residential lots.5 Whitis has already obtained a discharge
permit from the Texas Department of Environmental Quality and established Bell County
MUD #3 to facilitate the development of infrastructure on the property. 6

SECTION ONE – JOINT APPLICANTS HAVE NOT MET THEIR BURDEN TO ESTABLISH NEED.
II.       NEED: PURA § 37.056(C)(2)

          a. S&P Study: Conclusions without Sources

        To establish need, the Joint Applicants’ star witness was not present at the hearing.
Both the Permian Basin Reliability Study (“PBRS”) and the 2024 Regional Transmission Plan
(“RTP”) rely almost exclusively on the 2022 S&P Global Permian Basin Study (“S&P Study”)
to establish the forecasted load needs in the Permian Basin.7 While both the PBRS and the RTP
mention the S&P Study, a complete copy of the study was not included with the application.

        Neither Joint Applicant conducted an independent study to confirm that the S&P’s
forecasted load had been accurate during the 2022-2025 period, nor could they explain why
the forecasted average load nearly doubled between 2029 and 2030.8 Sixty-one percent of the
forecasted load was not confirmed by contract in 2022, including a staggering fifty-five percent
from Transmission Service Provider attestation letters alone. Joint Applicants did not verify
that the now four-year-old attestations remained accurate, nor did they offer the full S&P Study
into the record for others to confirm or criticize.

       The S&P Study predicted an 11,419MW increase from 2029 to 2030, and only a
2,741MW increase from 2030 to 2038,9 and the record does not contain an explanation for an
explosion of need in 2030 followed by virtually no growth in the following eight years. When

         b. PUC Staff Testimony:

       PUC Staff acknowledged that the Legislature and Commission have already recognized

25.370, and Staff further agreed that the load forecasting underlying this Application was built

ground” change, a reevaluation of load demand is warranted.14
         c. Independent Need

       The Permian Basin Reliability study established the three import paths, one of which
involves the transmission line in this case, which is a portion of Import Path 2.15 In October,
2024 the Commission identified the need for Import Path 2 with a target date in 2038. On
April 24, 2025, the Commission also approved a 2030 completion date in the RTP.16 Both
Commission actions rely on the same load forecast, as do the Joint Applicants.17 The only
evidence before the Court supports the construction of all three import paths as a single
comprehensive project. However, the Court is limited to determining what is in the scope of
the Application and whether the Bell East to Big Hill portion of Import Path 2 has
independently met the statutory requirement to establish a need for the project. On cross-
examination, the Joint Applicant panel admitted that it had not performed a partial build study

        In his cross examination, Mr. Gurley explained that he assumed TPL-001 mandated all
three import paths to address a “N-1-1” event.20 Mr. Gurley’s reliance on TPL-001 does not
establish a project-specific need for the Bell East-to-Big Hill line. Mr. Gurley acknowledged
that he was assuming TPL-001’s N-1 and N-1-1-type requirements supported ERCOT’s

ERCOT studied P0, N-1 conditions, selected generation-outage-plus-N-1 events, selected
345/138-kV-transformer-plus-N-1 events, and maintenance-outage scenarios.22 That is not a
generic “N-1-1” showing, and it is not a study isolating the need for this individual line. TPL-
001 may explain ERCOT’s planning framework, but like the PBRP and RTP, it does not prove
that Bell East-to-Big Hill is independently required. Like the Commission in its approval of
the PBRS and RTP, Joint Applicants exclusively relied on the conclusions of the S&P Study,
and have not met their burden to establish a specific, independent need for the Bell East to Big
Hill line that stands on its own.

        d. Conclusion – Need
        Joint Applicants failed to establish a reliable, quantifiable, and independent need for
the Bell East to Big Hill line under PURA § 37.056(c)(2). The application and record rely on
too many assumptions. When combined with clear evidence of meaningful changes to elements
of the S&P Study load forecast, PUC Staff’s testimony supports a reevaluation of the need of
Import Path 2. On the basis of failing to establish need, the Court should deny the CCN
Application.

III.    PURA § 37.056(C)(4) CRITERIA

recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, and the
probable improvement of service or lowering of cost to consumers. This brief will not address
all of these factors, and its silence should not be considered adoption or endorsement of the
Joint Applicant’s or any of the Intervenors’ positions on the factor.

        a. Community Values

the idea that the expressions of community values have not been fully and meaningfully
considered. The Commission should, therefore, strongly consider the expressed community
values when making the decision of which route is ultimately selected.

IV.     ROUTING CRITERIA – 16 TAC § 25.101(B)(3)(B)

         The Commission must “address the criteria in PURA §37.056(c) and considering those
criteria, engineering constraints, and costs, the line must be routed to the extent reasonable to
moderate the impact on the affected community and landowners unless grid reliability and
security dictate otherwise.”67 In addition, the Texas Administrative Code requires
consideration of whether routes parallel or utilize existing compatible rights-of-way and other
paralleling concerns, including the doctrine of prudent avoidance.68

        a. Prudent Avoidance
       The Commission’s policy of prudent avoidance is defined as “[t]he limiting of
exposures to electric and magnetic fields that can be avoided with reasonable investments of
money and effort.”69 Joint Applicants provided Dr. Edward P. Gelmann as a witness to speak
to concerns regarding exposure to electric and magnetic fields (EMF).

        While the policy of prudent avoidance commonly arises in the context of habitable
structures within 500 feet of the centerline of a proposed transmission line, a count of habitable
structures alone does not equate to a determination of prudent avoidance.70 Past Commission
Orders have shown that a route can have a higher habitable structure count and still satisfy the
Commission’s policy of prudent avoidance.71 In PUC Docket No. 38354, the Commission

                            SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT

       Because of the scale of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan and the aggressive statutory
deadline, nothing in this case should be treated as business as usual. To the Joint Applicants,
the conflux of these elements produced an application that presumed success without
independently establishing mandatory criteria for the project's need. To the Intervenors, none
of whom receive an identifiable benefit from the construction of this 765kV line, the PURA
routing factors have been thrown out of balance through the legislature's decision to sacrifice
some community protections for the benefit of the oil and gas industry in the Permian Basin.

        Even if the ALJs find that the project is needed, the route recommendation should not
default to traditional factor weighting. On this record, the proper balance is a route that gives
real weight to community values, existing and future land use, and preserving as much of the
original character of the affected land as possible. No other set of priorities comes close to
compensating for the burden placed on affected landowners.

          a. Prudent Avoidance

       The Commission's policy of prudent avoidance is defined as "[tlhe limiting of
exposures to electric and magnetic fields that can be avoided with reasonable investments of
money and effort."69 Joint Applicants provided Dr. Edward P. Gelmann as a witness to speak

increased cost compared to alternative routes, and satisfied the Commission's policy ofprudent
avoidance. 72 The Commission selected Route MK63 because it avoided cutting new corridors
through the Hill Country and avoided habitable structures and cities.73
